speechtext: PAYMENT OP 50 CENTS A BUSHEL TO PRODUCERS DELIVERING FLAXSEED TO WHEAT BOARD 1947^8

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make certain announcements that will be of interest to Canadian producers of oilseeds.
During the current crop year, 1947-48, the Canadian wheat board is buying flaxseed at a price of $5 per bushel basis the top grade of both eastern and western flaxseed at Montreal and Fort William-Port Arthur respectively. There is a ceiling price at this same level which fixes the price to Canadian crushers on domestic supplies. Any surplus over domestic requirements of seed and oil is available for export. Existing trading methods require the use of this surplus seed and oil in arrangements with the other countries so that Canada may secure supplies of other essential oils. Under present regulations, the producers who delivered flaxseed to the Canadian wheat board are entitled to participate in any net profits that may arise. It has become apparent, however, that this participation cannot be a clear-cut, commercial proposition when so many arrangements between countries are involved and the government has decided to calculate and pay out to producers the participation that would have been involved on a fair and reasonable basis. This action has the double effect of settling the producers' interest in the flax and freeing government agencies to use the surplus seed and oil in arrangements for other essential oils necessary to the whole Canadian economy. The government has therefore accepted the recommendation of the Canadian wheat board and will authorize that body to pay a fixed and final payment of fifty cents per bushel to those producers who have delivered or will deliver commercial flaxseed to dealers acting as agents of the board during the crop year 1947-48. This payment will involve distribution of about six million dollars to Canadian producers.
An announcement with respect to the handling and marketing arrangements for flax covering the crop year 1948-49 will be made at the earliest possible date.
With regard to rapeseed and sunflower seed, it is also the intention of the government to authorize the Canadian wheat board to buy these oilseeds in 1948-49 on the same basis as in 1947-48, namely, at six cents per pound basis the top grade of each, f.o.b. shipping points named by the board.

Do I understand the
announcement just made is in answer to the question I asked yesterday with regard to flax?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Yes.
That is that "flaxible" control.

Canadian government, changes have recently been made in connection with the signing-

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate

speechtext:
My question, of which I have sent a copy to the right hon. the Secretary of State for External Affairs is this: Have any changes been made in connection with the signing of our diplomatic representatives' credentials? If so, what are they?
(Text):
Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Secretary of State for External Affairs): The hon. member refers to three articles published in the newspaper Le Devoir on February 7, 9 and 11 and one said to have been published in the Chicago Daily Tribune on February 10 with regard to the effect of the letters patent constituting the office of governor general of Canada, which became effective on October 1, 1947, and he asks for an explanation in connection with the statements contained in those articles.
I received the hon. member's notice just three or four minutes before coming into the house, and I must confess that I had not read these articles. I have now obtained the articles and will give them careful consideration, but in the meantime I think it would be of interest, in view of the fact that the question has been raised, to place on Hansard the explanation which was given by the Prime Minister in a press release of October 1, 1947, dealing with the subject. I will then carefully consider the articles in question and see if there is any difference between what they contain and what was contained in the official statement; and if explanations are to be given as to differences I shall be glad to give them. The press release by the Prime Minister was as follows:
The Prime Minister, Mr. Mackenzie King, announced today that new letters patent governing the office and appointment of the Governor General of Canada had been signed by His Majesty the King on September 8, 1947, and countersigned by the Prime Minister of Canada. The new letters patent (the principal document relating to the office of governor general) come into force on October 1, 1947, and will supersede on that date the existing letters patent of 1931 (as amended in 1935) and the royal instructions of 1931.
2. The royal documents relating to the office of governor general had not undergone a careful revision since 1931. The Canadian government accordingly recommended to His Majesty the issuance of new letters patent consolidating the former documents and bringing them up to date.

3.	Apart from textual alterations designed to bring the new letters patent into line with constitutional developments and practices in Canada and within the commonwealth, the principal alterations may be summarized as follows:
(a)	By the introductory words of clause 2 of the new letters patent, the governor general is authorized to exercise, on the advice of Canadian ministers, all of His Majesty's powers and authorities in respect of Canada. This does not limit the king's prerogatives. Nor does it necessitate any change in the present practice under which certain matters are submitted by the Canadian government to the king personally. However, when the new letters patent come into force, it will be legally possible for the governor general, on the advice of Canadian ministers, to exercise any of the powers and authorities of the crown in respect of Canada, without the necessity of a submission being made to His Majesty. (The new powers and authorities conferred by this general clause include, among others, royal full powers for the signing of treaties, ratifications of treaties, and the issuance of letters of credence for ambassadors). There will be no legal necessity to alter existing practices. However, the government of Canada will be in a position to determine, in any prerogative matter affecting Canada. whether the submission should go to His Majesty or to the governor general.
(b)	The new letters patent revoke and supersede the existing letters patent and the existing royal instructions. The royal instructions have been incorporated in the new letters patent which have been issued under the great seal of Canada.
4.	No new commission of appointment will be issued to Viscount Alexander, the former letters patent having been revoked "without prejudice to anything having been done lawfully thereunder." Moreover, Viscount Alexander's present commission is a continuing one expressed to be subject to the existing letters patent "or any other substituted for the same."
5.	An appropriate proclamation will, as required by clause XVI of the new letters patent, be published today in the Canada Gaxette.
6.	Annexed to this statement is a copy of the new letters patent, with appendices giving the text of the documents in force prior to October 1, 1947.
That is the complete statement, and I will now table a copy of the letters patent and other documents referred to. As I said before, I will examine these articles to see whether they purport to make any statement of fact that would not be in conformity with the official press release, and give a further answer after I have made that examination.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
The house resumed from Tuesday, February 10, consideration in committee of Bill No. 3, respecting emergency measures for the conservation of Canadian foreign exchange resources-Mr. Abbott-Mr. Bradette in the chair.
On section 1-Short title.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
When the committee was last discussing this matter I had moved an amendment respecting the title of the act in which I had suggested the striking out of the word "emergency" so that the act would be known as the Exchange Conservation Act.
I pointed out at the last sitting of the committee that there was no question that, while the exchange situation beween us and the United States was in the nature of an emergency, nevertheless the emergency had now become chronic, and that any attempt to hide the facts of the case would delude the Canadian people in respect of the very essence of our exchange difficulties.
Since then, if anything, the exchange situation has been aggravated by the rapid and startling decline in the security markets of the world. These security markets are a barometer of world trade. They forecast accurately the situation to come, and show more than anything else the situation we are approaching, namely that we are moving from a sellers' to a buyers' market. In other words the international exchange position will be aggravated, as it was during the period of depression in the early part of the thirties.
When I say that I do not anticipate, nor is anything I say now to be so interpreted, that we are entering a period of depression or slump. That is not my intention, nor is it my
Foreign Exchange Conservation

belief. But I do say that the changeover from a sellers' to a buyers' market is upon us, and the first move has already been made. Therefore we shall be faced with selling our goods under different circumstances-some of them, I admit, in fortuitous circumstances in that those goods command a world market and are essential to the feeding of the world. On the other hand our essential metals are required for the making of the sinews of industry throughout the world, so that world industry may have the essential raw materials. We are in a fortunate position in that regard. But from the point of view of the over-all position, havipg regard to the rapid depression and the slump that has taken place on the security exchange, it can be said that we have moved into a different type of market, one in which pressure will have to be exercised in order to sell goods. That being so-and it is bound to happen sooner or later; every cyclical movement of trade develops in that way-exchange restrictions will have to be a continuing part of our way of life until such time a? world trade really gets to a state of equilibrium and regains some semblance of stability. It is merely wishful thinking to consider that that is likely to happen in the near future. Therefore I offered my amendment.
I have one further observation to make in this connection, and it is in direct reply to the hon. member for Acadia. He is perfectly correct when he says that I did support the Bretton Woods agreement. I believed, and I still believe, that some method of currency stabilization on an international level was necessary. I still believe there is at least a hope that that might take place. Therefore I supported the Bretton Woods agreement. The levels of currencies agreed upon under this agreement have proved to be completely unworkable. Instead of devaluating currencies, they were placed at an uneconomically high level in order to improve the trading position of the various members of the international monetary fund with the United States. This has made the whole Bretton Woods agreement unworkable.
My position now is that we should take steps to maintain our freedom in respect of the international monetary fund. It has been proved that under present regulations it cannot be made to work, or cannot be a workable instrument for the stabilization of international exchange. It has been proved that the rates fixed by the fund have no real connection with the actual value in the open market of the fund of the member countries. I feel that necessary steps should be taken; and if the fund will not bring reality into

its dealings, then either we should withdraw from it or should take such steps as will bring reality into our dealings with the fund.
I say that because there are just two alternatives in connection with currency stabilization, two ways in which it can be brought about. One is by the establishment of a gold standard; and I think it would be wishful thinking if we were to assume that in the chaotic situation of the world today any semblance of a fixed gold standard could be brought into being. The other way is by international agreement to stabilize currencies. I supported the Bretton Woods agreement in the hope that there would be some international agreement and that it would work. Unfortunately it has not proved to be workable.
As I see it, this situation is not likely to be temporary, despite the sanguine hopes of the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply. My reason for saying that is that our trading position is dependent upon world trade. If we are to control our currency, or at least attempt to control it, it will be a long long time before world trade gets into such a state of balance that these or some other regulations will not be necessary. If the government would free the Canadian dollar and abolish the foreign exchange control board these regulations would not be necessary. There are the two alternatives.
There is a third possibility which has been discussed at length in this house by myself, the Minister of Finance and others. I refer to the progressive devaluation of our dollar within the terms of the Bretton Woods agreement. I understand that we can devalue ten per cent and eventually a further nine per cent which would put our dollar at eight-one cents as compared', with the United States dollar. But even though we did that, I still believe that exchange conservation measures would be necessary.
We are deluding ourselves by thinking of this as a temporary measure. I have contended that part of this measure should have been adopted years ago. I do not want to repeat what I said the other night, that there are three parts to it. One is devaluation, and that action has not been taken. With the upset state of the world, with the majority of the world trading today under controls directly imposed by governments, unless we are prepared to take a long step and free ourselves completely from the foreign exchange control board, I do not see how we shall be able to get away from controls over currency of this nature for at least years to come. Therefore I move the amendment.

Three girls were journeying by bus from Kingston to the United States, over the international bridge, as they do once or twice a year. They were picked up by the customs officials. I want to pay a compliment to the customs officials, nearly all of whom are veterans of world war I. They are very courteous and gentlemanly, but they have to carry out their instructions under the foreign exchange control order. This girl was asked how much United States currency she had. When she came back across the border she expected that the $30 would be refunded, but the officials intimated that she had broken the law. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, so far I have not passed any comment on the bill which has been introduced. I wish that the Minister of Reconstruction were in his seat, because what I have to say concerns him.
I am one of those who wishes to see made effective the pronouncement some time ago of the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply that goods which are not made in Canada at the moment, but could be made here, should be made here. One of the schedules prohibits the importation of that type of goods. The minister has a program which I heartily endorse, namely, that of making more use of branch factories located in Canada of United States factories. The minister intends to encourage them to ship back to the United States many of their finished products made in Canada. I agree with that. The minister has an opportunity there which will be good for Canada, because there is a large number of United States plants, many of which I am thoroughly familiar with, whose plants in Canada are producing exactly the same material as they are in the United States. Some of these plants are located in Toronto, Hamilton and elsewhere in Ontario and Canada. I am going to encourage the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply to pursue that policy.
Much of the material that is now barred cannot be completed here unless more material and more machines come in. I want to assist the minister to the best of my ability to pursue his policy along that line in the hope that he

will save a lot of United States dollars by having material made in United States branch plants in Canada shipped back to the United States. I was thinking of one item, school furniture. At present, boards of education in Montreal, Toronto and elsewhere buy special school furniture in the United States. There are United States branch plants located in Canada. I have in mind one branch plant which makes a special line of school furniture. At the moment they need more machines to equip the plant to finish what they make. Until they are able to obtain certain equipment they will not be able to make the equipment our schools want.
The minister has had a lot of business experience. I hope he will see to it that some latitude is given to enable branch plants of United States firms located in Canada to finish the products that they can make. I repeat, I think the minister has something there and I should like to encourage him in every way possible to promote shipment to the United States of any material made in Canadian branches of United States plants, material which is exactly the same as that made in the parent plant in the United States. I cannot understand why a plant in the United States which has a branch in Canada should hesitate to encourage the importation into the United States of goods made in their Canadian plants. If that were done we would save a lot of United States dollars, and it would be doing no injury to our friends across the line.
When I take part in a debate I always try to add something worth while. Because of my long business experience I believe the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply has something in that program. I want to support him in that regard.
There are one or two other matters on which I should like to speak while I am on my feet. I should like those who have to do with issuing permits to use their best judgment in that regard. Do not ask busy men, big business managers, sales managers and their advisers, to come down to Ottawa to obtain a permit for some small item. I hope that in working out the program the two ministers have in mind, busy men will not have to come here for everything if a letter will do. I have no doubt that the department has officials who will be available to determine at once, even from a good letter, whether they should issue a permit or not. I hope consideration will be given to these busy men. They find it difficult enough to make a go of business without being harassed in coming down here to get a permit for a small item. Perhaps that is another way the two departments can assist in saving United States dollars. When the

________________Foreign Exchange Conservation
matter is laid clearly before the department I hope there will not be too much difficulty in getting a permit.
I wish to say to the Minister of Finance that Canadians generally want to assist him in saving United States dollars. I think everybody is imbued with the idea that it is necessary to do that. How can we assist him? I think Canadians want to help him. We all realize that we must cut down on what we buy from the other side. On the other hand we must enable those who are producing in Canada equipment containing something produced in the United States to be able to finish that equipment. If someone asks for a permit for a small machine or a small part of a machine to assist in making his product- for instance, school furniture-or some small part to complete the equipment which when completed could be exported back to the United States, thus bringing in United States dollars, I hope the two departments will use their best judgment to help business. I think most people really want to do the best job they can for Canada under present conditions. That is the spirit we all should have.
I wish to mention one further item, namely, stone. Many of the schools in the big centres use a great deal of Indiana limestone and other special types, and additions to some schools are planned. No one knows better than do the two ministers that two different types of stone cannot be used in the outside walls of a school without spoiling the whole symmetry of it. I do not know just what can be done. We do not want to import any more stone than necessary. But if a case like the one I have mentioned should arise, I suggest to the two ministers that they see to it that no trouble occurs. If it is a whole new school building that is planned, they should see to it that the school is built wholly of Canadian material, if it is available or if it can be substituted. But where a school is partly built and an addition is being made, I suggest that * some judgment be used in deciding whether the material required to build that addition should be admitted or not. At the moment I do not know whether it is admitted. I hope the best expectations of the government will be realized and that as much foreign exchange as possible can be saved. I for one want to help in achieving that objective.

speechtext:
I want to say a word on the amendment, and to remind the committee that the tenor of it is to point out that this bill is likely to be on the statute book for some time. With that wise caution which nearly all lawyers develop in the course of their practice the minister said he was "not going to attempt to hazard any prophecy or guess as to how long we
Foreign Exchange Conservation

might have to continue some kind of proper action to conserve our exchange and reserve position." I notice that his colleague, the Minister of Reconstruction, is still unrepentant about his use of the word "months", because he is 'reported to have used' it again in Halifax a night or two ago. I want to point out that this bill has no time limit on it, although the foreign exchange control bill, to which we made so much objection, did have a time limit. I believe it has only a little more than a year to run.
I want to point out again-I intend to say it in season, and perhaps the minister will sometimes think out of season-that this is a bill conferring arbitrary power of a kind absolutely foreign to all the professions of the party opposite. I am sorry that the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) has left the chamber; he was in his seat earlier. I was proposing to ask him, in view of the things he has had' to say about Liberalism, what he has to say about this arbitrary power. I should like to point out again that no matter in what temporarily pleasant hands arbitrary power is placed, it is still arbitrary power.
In December when we were here I ventured to make a prophecy. I ventured to say there would be little demur or protest from the business community, and I said the reason was that they would be afraid to come here. I do not often venture into the realm of prophecy, but I have had that one proved to my entire satisfaction. One of my friends tells me that he went to something like a dozen business firms to get some comment from them. Not one would say a word. And who is to blame them? After all, they may have to come down here next week to try to make some terms with the minister. I want to say again -and I hope my friends in the business community will hear me-that this is arbitrary power of the very kind that existed in Germany. I do not intend to talk about national socialism and all that kind of thing, but power is power. I want them to know that this is the same kind of power that the businessmen in Germany welcomed and thought would not hurt them a great deal. Indeed, for a while they thought it went nicely and even ministered to their profit. In the end they found that arbitrary power was not a pleasant thing.
I have just one further word to say. The gentlemen to my immediate left, even in the somewhat extreme suggestions which in our opinion they have from time to time made as to the exercise of power, have never I believe suggested a power like this, where one man has it in his hands to make or

unmake any business which has, as so many have, the need of substantial imports from the United States. Therefore we have a government today which is going beyond even socialistic doctrines so far as they would be applied at the present time by the gentlemen to our left. I ask the business community to remember that. I understand their difficulty at the moment, but I remind them again that when this sort of thing begins you can never tell where it will end.

Then I turn to a statement by Mr. Bryden, of the North American Life Assurance Company, who was a graduate in commerce and finance and got his training from the same sources from which Mr. Rasminsky of the Bank of Canada received his training. Mr. Bryden states:

A moment ago the minister replied to the hon. member for Acadia who had stated that there w'as more to the Hyde Park agreements than meets the eye. I have reason to believe that the Hyde Park agreements and the later arrangements made between Canada and the United States have had some influence upon this bill. I want to remind the house that the other day I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs if there was anything more to the Hyde Park agreements than the house already knew. However, the OttawA Citizen of February 7 had this to say:
The Washington correspondent of the Evening Citizen. Mr. Peter Inglis, however, has found that the senate committee on small businesses is in possession of much more "evidence."
He then goes on to discuss the whole matter, and he deals with the problems that confront the Canadian people because of this bill and other measures that are before us, such as the Geneva trade agreements. He points out that arrangements have been made between the two countries which have never been formalized or, as he puts it, have never been coded; nevertheless they are in the archives of the two nations. ment recognizes Canada as the forty-ninth state in the matter of receiving imports such as oil and steel, nevertheless, and again I quote his words:
-it offers Canada no apparent help in her present dollar difficulties.
On other occasions we have contended that it was unfair to apply the non-discriminatory clauses of the Geneva trade agreements to this particular bill. But the fact remains that in one section of the bill it is stated that permits will not be issued unless in the opinion of the minister they are necessary or hardship will result. We have seen no evidence since the minister assumed charge of his department that he has a mind which is receptive to other people's opinions. Apparently he is quite opinionated. We find that generally he has made up his mind before he comes into the house and there is no use offering any argument here. He contends that everything in this bill is all right, but the fact is that these non-discriminatory clauses are working hardship on some businessmen.
A short time ago the hon. member for Davenport said that he hoped the big business men of Canada would not be inconvenienced by having to come to Ottawa to see officials in order to get permits. I submit that it is infinitely more important that the small businessman be not required to do that. The big businessmen can afford to hire emissaries; they have expense accounts and they can send their people down, but the small businessmen have no possible way of getting down here, and, as someone suggested the other day, having a cup of coffee with the Minister of Trade and Commerce, a glass of Scotch with some other people, and a dinner with someone else. In looking through the bill I cannot find any section which would cover the illustration I want to give, but the fact is that the particular item has been banned. A small businessman in my city has been running a little shop where he sells goods. He is a good businessman and he has been able to get many customers. He recently took on the agency for the Norge and Magic Chef cooking ranges which use propane or bottled gas. Because of his aggressive sales policy and the fact that he was located in a
fMr. Bentley.]
section of the country where there was an immediate response because of a shortage of other fuel such as electricity and so on, he was able to build up a fair business. In the early stages he could handle the delivery of the bottled gas with his own truck, but later on the business developed to the point where he had to keep larger quantities of this propane gas in store in order to assure a continuity of service to the people to whom he had sold stoves. This meant a heavy investment. To a big businessman the investment may have represented only peanuts, it may have represented only the cost of a couple of trips to Ottawa, but it was a large investment for this man to make. He now finds that he cannot import Norge or Magic Chef stoves from the United States, and that it is difficult to get propane gas. His investment is lying idle, or mostly idle, because he cannot store the stuff. He could have bought the stoves from Great Britain, but he is not allowed to do it. The British trade commissioner wired on, December 19 that these cooking ranges are on the prohibited list from Great Britain.
We are supposed to be dealing with the principle of the bill, and I contend that that prohibition is unfair. The only item I can find that applies to this is item ex 446a on the last page of the newly printed bill.

I think the minister should give consideration to some of these things. We want British goods over here. Our people have indicated their willingness to use these commodities. Our merchants have indicated their willingness to merchandise them in this country. A majority of this House of Commons has indicated belief in private enterprise and private initiative. Surely things should not be done that hamper initiative simply because some other nation desires the application of the non-discriminatory clauses contained in the Geneva agreements.
I should like to refer to a speech made in this house by the Minister of Finance, who said, when asked why he applied these nondiscriminatory clauses:
While it possibly could not be called a fetish with them-

That is the United States.
-it is a principle to which great importance is
attached.
I have been suspicious of what has been going on in the last few years, and I believe that we are actually being sold to the United States. Before we go any further with it I should like to know the terms of sale. I can see no earthly reason for banning British goods from this country. In this connection I should like to quote a reprint from the Toronto Globe and Mail, appearing in the Vancouver News-Herald of January 30, 1948. It says in part:
The intent of the program was to discourage purchases from the United States. But the same bans were applied to the soft currency countries, which were thus deprived of any chance to repay us in goods for the credits we had extended them. Mr. Abbott and his brain trust, in their eagerness to keep Washington happy, evoked a "non-discrimination" clause. Its effect has been to discriminate most harshly both against the Canadian people who have to pay the cost and against those nations we should be seeking to help.
The British board of trade, for instance, released on December 11 a list of manufactured articles available for export. Of 86' items on the list, 39 were under the import ban, 13 were restricted by quotas, 21 were subject to 25 per cent excise tax and 13 could be imported only under permit.
I submit that the whole thing is unfair and that parts of this bill should be revised by the minister to make it acceptable to the Canadian people as a whole and to this house as representative of the people.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
Perhaps I had better answer now one or two points raised by my hon. friend. First he referred to the Hyde Park agreement and intimated that this bill is in some way tied in with benefits we got from the United States under the Hyde Park or some other agreement. That is not the case. The Hyde Park agreement during the war actually resulted in the purchase in Canada by the United States of about one and a quarter billion dollars worth of goods and that accounted in substantial measure for the very strong position in which our dollar reserves were at the end of 1945.
I have answered my hon. friend's point as to the non-discriminatory clause on two or three occasions. As to the United States making almost a fetish of non-discrimination, we do too. No country has a greater stake in the principle of non-discrimination than has Canada and being of that opinion we feel that we should set an example. I have repeated time and again that on balance this does not prejudice exporters from soft currency areas. On the contrary it helps them enormously. But because of the quota system,
while that results in severe restrictions of United States imports, it permits a tremendous expansion of importations from soft currency countries.
As to propane gas type stoves and heating and cooking apparatus, importations are very heavy running into several million dollars.
I cannot say offhand how much of that is represented by the propane type of gas stove, but the proportion would be substantial. We have to select some things to exclude. The government has no illusion that this will be a popular measure. We fully realize that, in essence, it is bound to be unpopular, but it is one of those things which the government has to do on occasion. There is no doubt that this is not a vote-catcher. I have no illusions that we are going to get a lot of votes by this measure. But the measure is an unfortunate necessity. If we are going to accept responsibility for the restriction of imports, we have to restrict something; we have to select the less essential commodities which are in reasonably good supply in Canada. I daresay that propane gas type stoves are produced here.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS

That business has grown

If some means can be found of affording some relief there, well and good, but, as I said at the outset when I announced this policy on November 17, there are bound to be some hardships and inconveniences. We have tried to make them as little as possible. These articles on the prohibited list have been selected with the greatest care. We have endeavoured to select articles which were imported primarily from United States dollar areas rather than from soft currency areas. I think we have been pretty successful in that, because I am informed that if imports were on the same scale as last year the whole prohibited list would exclude only one and a quarter million dollars worth of goods from the United Kingdom, which is negligible compared with the total importations. That is the position with respect to the non-discriminatory question. It is, of course, non-discriminatory. We believe strongly in that principle. It is not as non-discriminatory in fact as it is in form. We have maintained the principle of non-discrimination, and I for one believe and the government believes that it is in the interests of Canada that this principle should be maintained.

no avail, bon. gentlemen in the other place were able to enforce upon the government a certain time limit. I think the Minister of Finance, who at that time may have been a parliamentary assistant, said that they would not make any changes.

speechtext: I was Minister of National Defence at the time.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
But changes were made. I remember that in a corridor conversation he said that changes would not be made, but changes were made.
The second point I wish to make in regard to the use of the word "emergency" is that there is nothing curative in the present regulations in this bill. It is entirely as I have said twice in this house, very much like a patient who takes insulin, which keeps him alive from day to day but cures nothing. At least the minister should point out to the committee just how or where he expects our exchange position to be righted, and how he expects to look forward to having the condition remain righted and the controls removed at the same time. So far as one can see, these controls will be with us probably forever unless some adventitious event occurs and helps the government out of its predicament. The method of cure which many of us on this side of the house prefer is, of course, the more normal and natural one, the one which has worked in times gone by, namely, devaluation, perhaps step by step and within Bretton Woods, as I believe we shall be allowed to do. The question now is whether one wants the government to put on selective controls; whether the people want the government to prohibit this item or that or put it on the quota basis, or whether the people themselves, under the natural working of exchange, allow our dollar to go to the discount at which it is entitled to sell because of our prodigal buying. Do they want the government to tell them they may have this and that, or are we to continue under conditions as they have always operated in a free economy? There is not very much difference except as to who is to do the dictating, the individual or the government.
Are we to allow the normal method of economic law to work the situation out and to right it permanently and give it a permanent, self-righting cure? Is the government to decide whether we shall have $150 each to travel in the United States, or whether we can spend $10 for lettuce in the cold season? Personally I would much rather spend $10 for lettuce in place of being told by the government that I could have $150 to go to the United States.
The people of Canada do not want to be told how they may spend $20 or $25. They want to be given a certain freedom.
One generation may have been raised without lettuce and fresh vegetables in the wintertime. Another generation may have different ideas. Surely people can spend their own money the way they want to spend it, and if the government makes so much United States exchange available per capita, let the individual spend it as he wishes.

I am always very glad to bow to your ruling, Mr. Chairman, but the question is whether or not the word "emergency" is applicable in this particular bill or whether it is not. sources in order to buy United States products in the event that when the controls finally did come about, which were so well known to all these importers, they would then simply coast along for a while and give the minister's exchange account the appearance of having been temporarily righted, perhaps without too great hardship to the people.

Mr. Chairman, if you are going to rule against me I am forced to obey your ruling. What I should like to know is this. If these regulations are entirely of a temporary or emergent nature, as I assume the minister will suggest, how are we to re-establish our credit in the United States? States exchange, we shall be in a position to make repayment? As long as these regulations do not cure but merely keep alive, I do not feel that we are likely to reestablish our credit. The minister should point out to us what there is of a curative nature here which will, over the long term, keep the Canadian dollar in balance at some appropriate level.

What is to be the position of the Canadian dollar, first, vis-a-vis sterling and, second, vis-a-vis the United States dollar? In times gone by, when we were not on the gold

standard, when you could not exchange all currencies at parity, we occupied a midway position. Should we be successful in restoring the triangular trade basis on which we functioned for so long in the past, when are we to readjust our currency so that we can get back to that normal position? subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS

In the meantime the whole economy of Canada is being put through the strains of severe regulation for a possibly unrealistic objective.
This is from the Montreal Gazette, which was discussing reviews made by two publications, one from the sterling area and one from the dollar area, The Economist and the United States News. They are on different sides of the water; they both have statistical branches, and so on, as well as economists of no mean skill. In the meantime the whole economy of Canada is being put through bte strains of severe regulation for a possibly unrealstic objective.

just as much interested in the small businessman as in the big businessman. I have been in business all my life, and businessmen and employment are my interest. I want to repeat what I said before, that I hope the two departments who have to handle this problem, which is a big problem, will try to work out some method whereby businessmen, large or small-it makes no difference to me, as long as they are employing labour-who find it necessary to ask for an explanation in regard to any regulations, will not always find it necessary to come to Ottawa. When I was speaking a few moments ago I had in mind two men, both large employers of labour. One has 670 men in his plant; the other has about 500. Both these men found it necessary to come to Ottawa, where they remained for about two days. They were treated very well by the departmental officials. From what they told me I am glad to learn that we have officials like those who discussed the problems of those two men, because both those gentlemen went back happy and satisfied, with their troubles eliminated.
What I had in mind was some method whereby such people could write to Ottawa, whether they were big businessmen or small, and have the department here unravel their difficulties without its being necessary for them to come here in person. I know what big businessmen have to do. A man with 670 employees believes it is his duty to be on the job every minute possible. It is no easy task to manage a company employing that many men, and to look after the products they produce. That is what I had in mind. I want both departments to make it as easy as they can for those who are seeing that the wheels of industry turn. I do not want the hon. member for Swift Current to get the impression I am not just as much interested in the small businessman as he is, or anyone else. That is not what I was trying to point out. I was talking for employers of labour, and I shall never cease talking for men who give other men employment.

I should like to ask the minister if he or his officials have made any investigation to ascertain whether United States funds can be saved by using Canadian National railway lines wholly within Canada rather than subsidiaries in the United States. I ask that question because last year in the railway committee I asked Mr. Vaughan, president of the Canadian National Railways, what the operating expenses of the Canadian National were on the line that runs from a point near Island Pond, Vermont, to Portland, Maine, and he told me the expenses amounted to $2,674,000. This year I put on the order paper a question asking if that amount was paid in United States funds. I was informed that of that amount, $2,348,482 was paid in United States funds. I am not in a position to say-and this may be looked into further-how much of the gross earnings was paid in United States funds. However, I believe that if the minister looks into the matter carefully he will find that a great proportion of the amount spent on that subsidiary of the Canadian National Railways running to Portland was paid in Canadian funds, while the operating expenses were paid in United States funds.
A dispatch from Ottawa appearing in the-Telegraph-Journal on November 28 last states:
The action of the Canadian National Railways in lowering export freight rates to Portland, Me., is in direct conflict with Canada's austerity program, it was admitted here today by officials of the foreign exchange control board. The belt-tightening program is to conserve United States dollars. The C.N.R.'s action will mean a depletion of this country's holdings of American dollars.

I do not wish to read further from this press report, but I would suggest that if the minister has not examined into the possibilities of saving United States dollars by having the trade of our country go through Canadian rather than United States ports, and particularly the port of Portland, the matter might well be looked into by him.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: I shall take note of my hon. friend's remarks and look into the matter.

speechtext:
Before eleven o'clock last Tuesday night, when discussing this bill I brought up the question of prohibitions against soft currency countries, and the minister gave a reply, but it was then too late to discuss the matter further. A few minutes ago the minister made further reference to this matter.
The minister has emphasized the point that the amount of business lost through prohibition against soft currency countries is negligible. I think he would agree that, while the amount of business might be negligible today, it might be greatTy increased in the not too distant future. I receive publications from England, and I know that the production of the very things we are prohibiting today is being increased; that is, the amount of their production is being increased today and will continue to be increased considerably in the future. So that the amount of business might be increased considerably in a few months' time.
The other point the minister made was that the government stands solidly behind the principle of non-discrimination. The policy of non-discrimination is merely one principle contained in one article of the general Geneva agreements. I think the minister agrees that the important point is not so much that we do not violate one principle of the general agreement, but that we shall not violate the general agreement in its entirety.
That being so, I suggest that the minister will have to agree that if at any time we place against any one nation a prohibition that we are not called upon to place, under the general agreement, then in fact we are discriminating against that nation. It is all very well to give lip service to the idea of non-discrimination; but when you apply against a nation a prohibition that you are not called upon to apply, under the general agreements, then you are definitely discriminating against that nation.

The degree is not important; that is, it is not important as to whether it is a great deal of business or a small amount of business. That, as I say, is not important; it is a question of principle. And to substantiate my argument, let me quote from the Geneva trade agreement, article XIII of which creates the principle of non-discrimination. But article XIII is definitely modified by article XIV. You cannot take one article out of this agreement, and say that is the principle of it. You have to take the other articles which modify or are related to article XIII.
Article XIV gives the exceptions to the principle of. non-discrimination in several ways. Let me refer particularly to subsection 1 (b). Perhaps I should refer to the whole of section 1, which bears the heading, "Exceptions to the rule of non-discrimination". It states:
1. (a) The contracting parties recognize that when a substantial and. widespread disequilibrium prevails in international trade and payments a contracting party applying restrictions under article XII may be able to increase its imports from certain sources without unduly depleting its monetary reserves-
And this is the important part:

if permitted to depart from the provision of article XIII. The contracting parties also recognize the need for close limitation of such departures so as not to handicap achievement of multilateral international trade.
(b) Accordingly, when a substantial and widespread disequilibrium prevails in international trade and payments -
And I interject that certainly that is the situation today.
-a contracting party applying import restrictions under article XII may relax such restrictions in a manner which departs from the provisions of article XIII to the extent necessary to obtain additional imports above the maximum total of imports which it could afford in the light of the requirements of paragraph 2 of article XII if its restrictions were fully consistent with the provisions of article XIII, provided that
(i) levels of delivered prices for products so imported are not established substantially higher than those Tuling for comparable goods regularly available from, other contracting parties.	fi
I shall stop there. Perhaps the minister may be able to argue under that section that
the price level of goods we would be importing from Great Britain would be higher than the price level of goods from elsewhere. But I am not so certain he can substantiate that charge. I have seen quotations showing prices of articles we can import from Great Britain, and they compare favourably with prices of similar goods we can import from the United States today. But if the minister is to make

Foreign Exchange Conservation
that argument, namely, that we cannot import articles from Great Britain without a violation of article XIII, because the price level of goods is higher, then let me refer him to subsection (6) of article XIV which states:
The provisions of article XIII shall not enter into force in respect of import restrictions applied by any contracting party pursuant to article XII in order to safeguard its external financial position and balance of payments, and the provisions of paragraph 1 of article XI and XIII shall not enter into force in respect pf export restrictions applied by any contracting party for the same reason, until January 1, 1949.
I say when you take those two sections of article XIV you find they definitely modify article XIII which laid down the principle of non-discrimination. Therefore I charge that when you apply against a nation certain provisions which, under the agreement, you are not compelled to apply, you have discriminated against that nation. While the minister may like to give lip service to the principle of non-discrimination, I charge that today this government is unduly discriminating against the United Kingdom.
Another point is that the minister suggested that the benefit we would derive from this policy is far greater than the benefit we would derive from allowing these goods into the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: I said the benefits the United Kingdom would derive.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: I think that is perhaps a matter of opinion. If the minister could argue that the amount of production of these articles which today is prohibited could not be increased, that might be true. But in view of the fact that Great Britain today is greatly increasing the production of those very things, it might tell a different story. I again emphasize this fact, that if we along with the United States, as two great producing nations, try to force upon less fortunate nations agreements which are not to their benefit, we may find that we are building up a position which may very well cause international friction and create war. That will certainly not be to our benefit in the future.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS

in connection with these matters of price levels in Great Britain or in any other country.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: If you have not posed your argument in connection with non-discrimination in price levels in Great Britain, how can you say that in order to adhere to the Geneva trade pact you have to apply prohibitions against Great Britain? speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: I have not necessarily tied up the Geneva pact with that principle. I have reiterated time and again that Canada believes the non-discrimination principle is in its vital interest. Whether there is an escape clause in the Geneva agreement which would permit us to violate that principle for a twelve months' period is, in my judgment, not particularly relevant.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: The object of this bill is to conserve United States currency and the method being used to do this is to restrict imports from the United States. Naturally this will create shortages of many things in Canada. Is it not reasonable that, in order that we be not deprived of those things, our manufacturers, processors and growers should be given some guidance by the government? Is it not possible for the government to say to these people, "This restricted program is going to be in force for two months, for six months, for two years or for ten years"? Surely the government has some policy under which it can say to our growers and manufacturers that this will be in effect, say for at least a year? Does the government still say that it has nothing to give to the people of this country in the way of guidance as to what they should do?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: The difficulty with these committee discussions is that hon. members pop in and out of the chamber. I answered that question on Tuesday evening and again this afternoon.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: The answer is that there is no guidance to be given to the people of Canada?

It is quite evident that a great deal of discretion will be exercised under the provisions of this bill by departmental officials here in Ottawa, officials of the Department of Finance and the Department of Trade and Commerce. subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS

speechtext:
That will help a great deal, but the main difficulty is under schedule I which covers the power to deal with hardship cases. Practically all the cases that have been submitted to me come under schedules I and II and it was those cases I had in mind.

of particular hardship. I think it is fair to say that the great majority of those cases will already have been disposed of. Under the orders that exist now and under the statute as proposed that discretion must be exercised by myself. In practice, the way it is handled is this. The facts are submitted to a special committee, headed by Mr. Taylor. The facts are first taken by an official, either by correspondence or otherwise; then considered by this committee which has been set up by me, and that committee makes recommendations. In most cases I have accepted their recommendations where particular hardship has been shown. If there are circumstances which are very unusual they will sometimes discuss them with me first before consideration by the committee. I think it would be quite possible to have men collect the relevant facts, say in Vancouver, and send them here by wire or air mail for consideration by the committee, and by myself, if necessary. But I am afraid that in the very nature of things the discretion is one which has to be exercised here. I would find it difficult to delegate a general power to make these exceptions.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have an amendment to offer to this section. It concerns section 3 (1) of the bill. However, before offering my amendment, I should like to make a few remarks in support of it.
When closing the debate on second reading, the minister said that the principle of the bill was very simple. Its use was to apply import restrictions in order to conserve United States dollars. Yet, in no portion of the bill do we see any mention of United States dollars. As a matter of fact, except for the short title, and the title itself, the bill does not suggest that it is meant for the purpose of regulating exchange at all. If anyone reads the bill, without the explanation given in respect of it by the minister on second reading, he would say it was a bill intended for very high protection. As a matter of fact, the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard suggested that it might be used for that purpose.
Statistics found at page 882 of the Canada Year Book, 1947, show that in every year since 1919, including 1947, with the exception of four years Canada has had a favourable trade balance. And those years when we did not have favourable trade balances wrere 1920, 1929, 1930 and 1931. The total of these
Foreign Exchange Conservation

favourable trade balances, after deducting the unfavourable ones, is something in the neighbourhood of $9,000 million.
Even if we take into account payments made to foreign countries on account of private and public debts and obligations, which undoubtedly were paid out of these trade balances, it seems to me, even if we take these debts paid into consideration, that somebody, somewhere, somehow, must owe us a lot of money. In view of this apparent favourable situation, it is almost unbelievable -and I am sure it is unbelievable to the people in the country-that the government finds itself in the precarious position of presenting this remarkable bill to parliament at this time.
Our trade statistics show that in all these years we have always sold more to Great Britain, to the commonwealth and to other western European countries, than we have bought from these countries. I believe that is still so. And in fact, it has been more so in the last few years in spite of the British preference which, I believe, has been in force for some fifty years.
These statistics also tell us that during all these years we always purchased more from the United States than they purchased from us; in fact, we purchased considerably more than they purchased from us; and again especially in the last few years.
In his speech when presenting the bill to the house, the Minister of Finance explained how we were able to manage for years under this lopsided arrangement. He pointed out that Great Britain, the commonwealth and other countries to which we sold were able to sell enough to the United States in order to provide them with sufficient funds to pay us. And the way the minister explained it, it was a sort of triangular arrangement. It seemed to work nicely during many years, and especially before the first world war.
It now turns out that this triangle is by no means an eternal triangle, and that this vehicle upon which our foreign trade seems to have slid along fairly smoothly for years has now been smashed. It is interesting to speculate as to who should bear the blame for the smashing of this nice triangular arrangement.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
I am inclined to believe that no one in particular is to blame. We simply emerged into another new era of foreign trade and foreign relations necessitated by the technological and scientific advances on the one hand and war, destruction and
	, |
mistrust on the other. It seems to me that by force of these circumstances the world has lost its old banker, Britain. And, again by force of circumstances, and without anyone willing it, the United States has emerged as the world's banker. Without laying any particular blame on our good neighbour to the south, Uncle Sam, I am of the opinion that we find ourselves in this precarious position today because Uncle Sam does not measure up to John Bull as the world's banker. You see, besides being the world's banker. Great Britain was also the world's trader. She was a free trade country. She took goods from other countries which owed her; and if she did not need those goods for her own domestic use, or for any other use, she sold them wherever she could.
It seems to me that in thinking of world trade-and I argue that we would do well to think about that condition-and especially world trade before the first world war, perhaps we may now realize that the world owed a debt to Britain for managing the system of world trade quite well prior to the two wars. Without arguing in favour of going back to that system of world trade, it seems to me that, in order to revert to the fairly smooth working situation which existed before the wars, we would need a banker who is also a world's trader. And if Uncle Sam is to be that banker, whether he wills it or not, we have to go a lot farther than the concessions which have been made under the Geneva trade agreement.
The present bill attempts to rectify the siluation by conserving United States dollars. At the same time it endeavours to do this in a spirit of non-discrimination, as set forth in the Geneva agreement. In other words, the bill is drawn in accordance with the terms and spirit of the provisions of this agreement. I know that the minister in his address in presenting the bill on second reading did not rely upon the terms of the Geneva agreement. He tried to justify the non-discriminatory elements in the bill upon its own merits. But I may say I am quite sure the people in the country understand that the non-discriminatory feature of the bill is there because we wish to live within the terms and spirit of the Geneva agreement. That is why this bill is put forward as a non-discriminatory bill, and it is my opinion that, because of the inclusion of that principle, the bill will fail in its objectives. Even with the Geneva agreement, we still have time to enact a measure that would deal with this serious situation. It is true that it would have to be discriminatory, but it might remedy the situation.

The hon. member for Acadia spoke on this matter on Tuesday and again this afternoon. He referred to articles XII and XIII and he read portions of article XVI. In order to have the story complete, I think we should have on the record the pertinent portions of articles XII and XIII. Article XII is the article which permits a signatory nation to the agreement to enact measures such as the one we are enacting at the present time. I shall read only the words which are necessary in order to make my meaning clear, which are:
Notwithstanding the provisions of paragraph 1 of article XI, any contracting party, in order to safeguard its external financial position and balance of payments, may restrict the quantity or value of merchandise permitted to be imported.
And again:
(i) to forestall the imminent threat of, or to stop, a serious decline in its monetary reserves.
The pertinent part of article XIII reads:
No prohibition or restriction shall be applied by any contracting party on the importation of any product of the territory of any other contracting party . . . unless the importation of the like product of all third countries or the exportation of the like product to all third countries is similarly prohibited or restricted.
Even to that non-discriminatory clause there is an exception. The hon. member for Acadia placed on the record the pertinent words in article XIV which provide an exception to that rule of non-discrimination set forth in article XIII. I am of the opinion that we could afford to use discrimination in order to balance our exchange with the United States. The minister said that Canada or the government is proud of the stand taken in applying, not discrimination, but rather non-discrimination in connection with this bill, and that we want to set an example. That is all very well and I commend him for his fine spirit, but the question is whether we can afford to take that attitude. I submit that we cannot. Even the United States is not loath about enacting a law which is against the spirit of the Geneva agreement. Just a few days ago I read in Foreign Trade, a publication of the Department of Trade and Commerce, issue of January 31, 1948, the following which appears on page 225:
The United States treasury department has ruled that the Canadian excise tax, imposed on November 18, 1947, is part of the freely offered price in Canada. Under the present United States customs laws, therefore, this tax must be included in the value for duty purposes of goods, subject to this tax when imported into the United States.
I submit that that attitude on the part of the United States is contrary to the provisions of article VII, section 3 of the Geneva agreement, which reads:
3. The value for customs purposes of any imported product should not include the amount of any internal tax, applicable within the country of origin or export, from which the imported product has been exempted or has been or will be relieved by means of refund.
In view of our precarious position, I submit that we cannot afford to set an example of non-discrimination. It is only discrimination that will overcome the difficulties in which we find ourselves. It seems to me that in order to balance our foreign financial position, in order to overcome our present monetary disequilibrium, in view of the statistics which have been quoted, we must restrict imports from the United States and all other countries which demand hard currency and encourage imports from countries which are willing to take our goods and which, by the way, already owe us a lot of money. I think we could very well apply the principle of discrimination to this bill, and therefore I beg to move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre:
That subsection 1 of section 3 of Bill No. 3 be amended by inserting after the word "Canada" in line nine on page one of the said bill, the following words:
"From any country requiring gold or currency of the United States of America in payment or settlement of their purchase price."
That subsection would then read:
No person shall import or attempt to import into Canada from any country requiring gold or currency of the United States of America in payment or settlement of their purchase price any goods listed or of the classes described in schedules I, II or III.

I turn now to item 415(a) in schedule I, which covers "refrigerators, domestic or store, completely equipped or not." I know we are not talking about taxes under this bill. Nevertheless refrigerators carry a 25 per cent tax. My understanding is that the manufacturer in Canada of electrical refrigerators can bring in all the parts he wants. In other words, the 25 per cent tax is to curtail production. But there is nothing in the regulations to curtail his importations. In other words, he has to cut down production. The 25 per cent tax is paid by young couples and veterans establishing homes, and the tax will slow up Canadian

I should like to have seen the electrical refrigerator manufacturers given a United States dollar quota similar to automobile manufacturers, and then you would not have needed this 25 per cent tax on refrigerators. They would get a quota of United States dollars for what parts they need. It is an established fact with all the leading refrigerator manufacturers in Canada that the refrigerator contains a certain United States content. There is nothing in the bill which says that a new company shall have a quota for bringing in parts, tools, machinery, and so forth. A United States firm might want to establish a branch in Canada. It may have lots of money in the United States and could send the parts in to its branch company. There should be some arrangement whereby new firms can get a quota on parts importations, even if it is only for a temporary period, until they can secure sources of supply in Canada to take care of their needs.
I do not know whether quotas have been set on automobiles imported from the United States. They are on the prohibited list but I understand there are to be quotas. I do not know whether it is to be a dollar quota to manufacturers or a car quota to dealers to bring in completed cars. Of course, if the quotas are equal in dollars to manufacturers and new dealers who have established themselves in business to be able to bring in Nash, Studebaker and other completed United States cars, the new dealer will be seriously handicapped. He could not get many cars if he gets only $210 a car. The importer of United States made cars who has no Canadian source of supply may be forced out of business, while the other dealers will still be kept in business, regardless of how severe the import quotas might be. I know that in my riding there is extreme hardship for four dealers, with a plant investment of $350,000, employing 3eventy-two men, and handling United States cars. They are now being practically put out of business. Their franchise is gone and their bank credit is practically gone.
I notice another item in schedule I, item 192 on page 8 of the original bill. I have not the reprint here. It covers insulation. Insulation, with the exception of fibre glass, is prohibited. I do not know why that one type of insulation has been permitted entry, while all the others have been barred. I called the department in regard to these items and asked
different people to try to find out why. I should like to know for my own satisfaction. We have refrigerator manufacturers and other people building houses and trying to insulate them. I asked the department why fibre glass was permitted to come into the country and other insulating materials were not. Finally I was told that somebody would call me back. You cannot expect everybody in the department to know everything, except the minister.
The individual to whom I was talking said that fibre glass was a much better insulating material. He said that it was a higher class material with much more heat resistance, and that is why it was admitted. I asked him what was the "K" factor of fibre glass. He said, "I do not get you." I said, "What is the 'K' factor of fibre glass?" He said, "I cannot tell you that." I said, "I can tell you that, because I have a book published under the authority of the Hon. J. L. Ilsley, M.P., Minister of Finance, in 1943, and on page 23 he lists the 'K' factor of these insulating materials." I might explain to the committee that the "K" factor has to do with heat resistance or conductivity of insulating material. Glass wool, which is fibre glass, has a "K" factor of [DOT]27; "Kimsul" and some other types of insulation that are prohibited have a "K" factor of [DOT]27, exactly the same. I told him that, and he said, "Fibre glass is used for certain types of refrigeration only; it is cut the size and it does not absorb moisture." That is all right. The minister might give somebody the right to import fibre glass for a particular type of refrigeration where there might be a certain moisture condition and where batts and other types of insulating material could not be used. Cork insulation is out because it is too hard to get.
Fibre glass was never used for insulating houses up to within the last few years.
