Machine-made tumblers, mostly tableware, come from the United States. If they are decorated when they come off the machine they are permitted to come in, but if they are decorated afterwards they are prohibited. The reason is that this bill is drawn solely on tariff items. Plain ware comes under one item and decorated ware under another. Before the war we used to get a lot of this ware from Belgium and England. Recently we seem to have cultivated the United States source of supply. Consequently they have allowed tumblers to come in from the United States. I cannot say whether we should or not, because I am not in a position to say whether we have enough in Canada or can get them from Belgium or not. But if tumblers come in from the United States, certainly we should allow the plain ones in. They cost twelve cents a dozen less, and in carload lots, which is the way they are bought, that is quite an item. This is another item that should be checked and rectified. These are not policy objections; they are schedule objections. As I said a while ago, they should have come under item 4, because some of them will create a real hardship.

I have nothing further to say on this schedule with the exception of that which was mentioned by the hon. member for Davenport this afternoon. I hope that limestone from Indiana will be permitted entry, so that the universities which are now expanding to take care of student veterans will be enabled to enlarge their institutions without spoiling their architectural appearance. I also hope that the Minister of Trade and Commerce, in his quite generous and thoroughly businesslike way, will give these universities permits for the necessary building material to enable them to accommodate the students they have received from the second war. That is all I have to say, Mr. Chairman. I could have put on a lot of questions, but that would take a lot of time. My questions are now on the record and we shall probably get the answers before the section is disposed of.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: I wish to go back to the question of permits under schedule III which, I think, are the most difficult and important. I do not know whether the minister would like to add something to what was said this afternoon just before the dinner recess. What we want to know is on what basis the permits are made; whether each case is being dealt with on its individual merits or whether there are certain general rules. We were told) that regulations were to be made. The minister might tell us whether these regulations have been made. If so, what are they? If not, why not, and just what the situation is at the moment.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
There is a variety of permits under schedule III. Permits covering new construction are issued) on a project basis. In other words, if a building project is approved a project number is given the over-all expenditure. When approved, individual permits issue automatically. And, as applied to the project, the sum total of the individual permits must not exceed the limit set in the project, but within that limit permits issue freely.
So far as individual items of equipment are concerned, we have rules applying to that. If it is a replacement of a worn-out part it will issue automatically. If it is a new machine, the needs of the situation are examined and it depends on whether a case can be made out or not.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
Will the minister permit a question? Is the

Foreign Exchange Conservation
minister going to put on the record certain regulations, or is he just going to give us the general description?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: Well, the only regulations today are the over-all permits affecting the automobile industry, both the manufacture andl the parts. But it is impossible to bring new construction projects down to an absolutely rigid 'basis. Generally speaking, the tests there are as to whether they will create important amounts of United States dollars; whether they are essential to the industrial life of Canada, such as hydro-electric plants; and as to the general purpose of the project. On several occasions I have said that projects which merely add to the comfort and convenience of the Canadian people are not granted permits; for example, moving picture theatres, office buildings or places of amusement are glaring examples of projects that are not granted permits.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: That is interesting to know after all these years.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: If my hon. friend will just keep quiet I shall be able to inform the hon. gentleman who asked1 the question. My hon. friend's interjections are always helpful, but if we could keep the discussion to one at a time, it would help. As far as manufacturing firms are concerned, the purpose is to encourage the use of Canadian facilities to the maximum extent. The arrangement with the automobile industry has been published. It is so framed as to encourage the maximum use of Canadian components as well as the maximum effort on the part of the industry to export and help us to obtain United States dollars.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
I wish to ask a question
of both the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Trade and Commerce. At the present time I presume we are carrying on under P.C. 4678?-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: That is correct.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: -and whatever regulations there are must be in P.C. 4678.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: That is correct.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
There are a great number of things in P.C. 4678 such as designate currencies, non-resident, foreign currency, sterling area countries, Canadian currency, United States dollars and so on, which go to the very root of the matter of these import controls; yet they do not appear at all in the bill. I presume they must, at some time or another, all be covered by regulations,
and regulations come under this section 3. My suggestion, and it is only a suggestion, is that, since those regulations must come before us some time, they ought to come before the house just as soon as possible so that we may deal with these matters which are the very meat of this whole bill. That is my first thought.
My second thought is directed to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. He suggested that permits will be issued under schedule III in the way of projects. I presume that, if it is decided that a certain project was a necessary one and was entitled to a permit, if it was an office building the limestone required may come in, as well as marble and steel. There would not be any end to the component parts of that building that might come in under that project permit. Does it give to the builder, the contractor or owner a choice of materials, or just what strings does the minister have on the things that come in under that permit?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: Before any project is approved, it is screened for United States content ; and where Canadian substitution is possible, any United States content is stripped from the project before it is approved. When the project is approved it has a list of materials to be imported from the United States, and a dollar value for those materials which has been approved by the officials responsible for the examination. But any project that is approved is approved only to the extent of permitting the import of materials absolutely necessary for the completion of the project.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
May I follow that up
by another question? As has happened and as will happen, suppose the minister is confronted with a project which is an office building and right next door he is confronted with another project which is partly mercantile and partly office building, what happens there?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
Neither one would be
approved.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
Inasmuch as in certain
places, I see buildings being torn down and people being thrown out of their offices, can we take it absolutely that if they are in either one of those categories the projects will not be allowed to go ahead?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: That is right.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
Is there not some way
that we could have before the house, and not so much before the house as before the
Foreign Exchange Conservation

people in business who may not be able to obtain them, the regulations which are to govern the minister's decision in respect of these matters in the future?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: It is much easier for anyone in doubt to write to the department and get a ruling on the case than it is for me to lay down definite rules.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: We shall have to get back to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Kindersley before long; but, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce has been brought into this discussion, I should like to express the hope that, some time before long, he will make a statement as to what is being done under his direction with regard to the positive side of this new program. We were told in November, when the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance made their famous announcements, and we have been told a number of times since, that this program is not just a restrictive one; that it consists not only of the kind of measures that are before us now under the direction of the Minister of Finance, but that there is also a positive program headed up by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. We have been led to believe that there is to be an expansion of industry as the basis for increased exports which, in the long run will improve our position greatly. In the debate on the second reading of this measure, the Minister of Finance indicated that the Minister of Trade and Commerce would go into the matter later and give us the positive side of the story; but I submit that we are still waiting for it. The Minister of Trade and Commerce is talking in the same restrictive terms that we get from the Minister of Finance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: We have this bill before us now.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: I am not particularly anxious that the Minister of Trade and Commerce make that kind of statement tonight, but I think he owes it to the house and to the country, some time soon, to give us some details on the positive side of the program.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: The question just raised by the hon. member is one we spent all afternoon on.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
I shall save you the trouble of asking it again. The attention of the department is being devoted actively to making use of any existing facilities in Canada. The department is also encouraging new projects which promise to be substantial earners of United States dollars or to add subfMr. Timmins.]
stantially to Canada's useful exports. That is the direction in which the efforts of the department are being directed, and with some success, I may say. We have arranged for the use of existing facilities which will provide for substantial increments of United States dollars.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: Can the minister give some details, indicating in what industries or in what facilities these developments are taking place?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: That is out of order.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: I question how far we should be led down side alleys of this sort, Mr. Chairman. This has nothing to do with this bill.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: It is an important part of the program. We have been waiting for it for three months.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: I mentioned a program of $50,000,000 of aluminum exports to the United States from facilities that are not now active. I could mention an accumulation of other groups of projects, but I think it would hardly help hon. members to decide about this bill.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: When shall we get that kind of discussion?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: I do not think you will ever get it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: That is a great reply for a member of the Liberal party to give in the parliament of Canada.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
Yes; and I am a member of it, and it is my turn. I contribute little, perhaps, and what I have to say now will be brief. A moment ago the hon. member for London was telling of the experience of some people who came to the border at Windsor. He was rudely contradicted by the Minister of National Revenue; and unfortunately that is becoming a habit with the minister, though he is the only member of the cabinet about whom I will say that. Lest he think everyone in his department is perfect, let me tell him that I crossed the border on January 25 at North Portal. I was going to the other side because of my health. My bank had communicated with the department and had obtained $400 for me. That took in my wife's $75 and my $75, so I did not get all the gravy that was going. I had my form H and everything else I should have had. The officer at North Portal said, "Have you $400"? I replied that I had. He said, "I will have to take it from you." He scared my wife to death; but I said, "Yes; you and who else?" Let us not think for one moment

Foreign Exchange Conservation
that these people the hon. member for London was talking about are all trained; and I hope they are not taking their cue from the manner exhibited' by the minister in this house tonight.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: I want to ask the minister one question on this point. What would be the reason for prohibiting the importation of certain very necessary things at this time, while at the same time there are no restrictions on the importation of United States films?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: That is a pretty general question. I believe my colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce is dealing with the film aspect of this matter. Some people consider that films are just as necessary a part of life as, shall we say, strawberries in January or some other things.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: Cabbages.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: Well, we are importing cabbages now. One purpose of this program is to interfere as little as possible with established businesses in Canada on which a great many people are dependent for their livelihood. I do not think anyone can deny that the entertainment industry, including the motion picture industry, is certainly not patronized only by the upper ten, or that it is an industry which employs a great many people, and that it would be neither wise nor even desirable to cut it off in that way. I believe the Minister of Trade and Commerce can give the committee some idea of what is being done with respect to the importation of films, but I would hesitate to believe that members of this committee would suggest that we should prohibit the importation of United States films, or, for that matter, of any films.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: They are a lot better than the films than the national film board get out.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: Negotiations are going on with the film industry which promise a substantial quid pro quo to offset the drain of dollars caused by the industry. I am not prepared to make a full announcement this evening, but I think I can say Canada will get good value from the industry in return for permitting the industry to take Canadian dollars across the line.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: Has any restriction at all been placed upon the importation of films from the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: Certain film materials and cameras are prohibited.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: But has any restriction been imposed yet on the films?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: No.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: A moment ago the Minister of Trade and Commerce spoke of various types of industry they were endeavouring to develop in Canada in order to save United States dollars. I just wonder if he will give particular attention to the possibility of developing the beet sugar industry in Canada. Last year we lost practically $28,000,000 in United States dollars because our beet sugar industry was not developed. If we really mean to get somewhere; if we really intend to develop industry in Canada, it is industry of this kind to which we must devote our attention, because there is no doubt this industry can succeed, and there is no doubt the Canadian beet sugar industry can save United States dollars if just a little common sense is shown in the management of that industry. But common sense was not indicated in the reply given me the day before yesterday by the Minister of Finance to a question I asked.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: Well, Mr. Chairman, could we get back to section 3?

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: I am most concerned about the reply just given by the Minister of Trade and Commerce to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, who brought up a subject with which the committee was concerned all afternoon. One hon. member after another taxed the Minister of Finance with the same question. This is a restrictive measure, one of the positive measures, one of the curative measures in this legislation. Now it is put up to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and he gives us the answer that there will never be the possibility of discussing this in the House of Commons. In other words, we must trust to him. I just want to draw a parallel to that answer, and I think it is apt in this case. Last evening I spent some hours in reading Mr. Trevor Roper's book entitled, "The Last Days of Hitler." In it he describes Mr. Goebbels' propaganda during the late war, by means of which the German people were kept happy year after year with his promise of the secret weapon. As I see it, this promise is the secret weapon of the Department of Finance and the Department of Trade and Commerce, and the Canadian people will never know what it is.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: I wish to say a word about the same question. As I understood it, the minister in effect said to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that the details of the positive side of the government's new program would never be known.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
He did not say that. *

Foreign Exchange Conservation

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: I did not say that.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
I have been a businessman myself, and I am not suggesting that the minister should come out and tell us all the details of this or that arrangement he has in view. But I am suggesting that we should not be left to learn in the newspapers some fine day that this or that has been done. I suggest that we are entitled to some general ideas, not just these vague pieces of optimism. I notice the minister was at it again the other evening, saying this would be only a matter of months. He might do well to learn a little from the Minister of Finance, who does not indulge in nonsense of that kind. I think we are entitled to some information, unless we are to believe that this arbitrary power has made the minister not only above himself but above us. There must be some information we can have and not, as I say, just these general observations.
Before I sit down, I want to ask one other question. I understood the minister to say that one of the industries to which United States dollars were being allowed was the automobile industry, and that this was being done on the basis of the amount of United States dollars which that industry was likely to bring into Canada. That is what I took down when the minister was speaking, and I thought that was what he said. If he wants to correct it I wish he would do so now.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
The particulars of the automobile regulations have been published in the press for the last four days, both in advertisements and in the news columns. I have not that information before me at the moment, though I can get it. I said it was a proportion of imports they were allowed in the standard period, plus a proportion of the money spent on complete automobiles imported, plus a certain proportion of the money recovered from exports. But surely my hon. friend reads the newspapers, and he must have read that if he has any interest whatever in the subject.
So far as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is concerned, if he saw the trade statistics for the last month which were published, and which I am sure are of interest to him, he would find that the increase in exports is very much larger than the decrease in imports. The exports did increase largely, while the imports were reduced, which is an indication that the program is in operation. And we hope that the future figures will indicate the same thing, namely a substantial increase in exports, while we bring about a reduction in imports.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: What are the increases in exports? Will the minister give us details?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: We issue press releases on that subject almost every day. Surely my hon. friend knows that.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: I am asking the minister, if he has those figures, if he will let us have them. We are discussing that now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: We are completely out of order.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: When will it be in order? I was told a minute ago, "never". I am asking the question again.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: Part of this discussion is certainly out of order, because we are dealing with Bill No. 3, emergency measures for the conservation of foreign exchange. Is the amendment carried?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
I wish to point out to the committee again that we are dealing with Bill No. 3, which is one sector of the dollar conservation program. It is a purely restrictive measure. I cannot say at the present time that it would be proper for me to speak about constructive measures which the government is taking, through the Department of Trade and Commerce and through other government departments, to increase our exports. But I do know, and I am certain that it would not be on section 3 of this bill.
.Mr. MACDONNELL (Muskoka-Ontario): Just a minute; we are discussing permits, and we have been asking the Minister of Trade and Commerce to tell us the basis upon which permits are being issued.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: It has not anything to do with export.	*

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: He has told us one of the bases of permits being issued-and I took this down-is the proportion of United States funds recovered by the motor industry. I want to know how the motor industry is recovering American funds. I do not think it is an unfair remark, for he himself brought it in as part of his argument. However, I will not press it. But I do wish to know what he means by saying that the automobile industry is producing American funds. If he is correct, where are the exports of motors going, which are producing American funds?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, all I can say is that it may surprise my hon. friend to know

Foreign Exchange Conservation
that the Canadian automobile industry is not a drain on balance-that is the industry manufacturing in Canada is not. It does not constitute a drain on American funds. Value of exports is in excess of value of imports. The net balance does not represent a drain.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: Does the minister mean a net balance in American funds?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: The net balance of exports.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: That has not anything to do with this.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: I say that it is much the same thing. However, it would take all evening to explain that to my hon. friend.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: All right, take all evening to do it.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
As a matter of fact, dollar exports to the United Kingdom at the present time are just as good as exports to the United States, in obtaining American funds, because the balance in excess of the loan is paid for in gold-that is American funds.
However, the point I make is that it seems to us that the industry is capable of contributing much more in American funds than it has been doing, and the regulations are framed with that in mind. I shall be very glad to get the regulations and either put them on Hansard or send them to my hon. friend. I have sent up for them. I am surprised that he has not read them. I think he will see they are definitely designed for that purpose.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: The minister said that exports to the non-dollar countries were paid for in gold. Does that mean that exports of automobiles from Canada to South America and England are paid for in gold?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: The minute gold is mentioned, my hon. friend pricks up his ears; the discussion is getting into his territory. The position is this, that certain amounts of credit are issued per month to the sterling countries. Everything above those amounts is paid for in gold. If we ship anything to the sterling areas in addition to the amount of the credit, it is just as valuable in United States dollars as though we shipped it to the United States, because it produces gold. That is probably too deep for the hon. member.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
What the minister said was that we allowed Britain so many credits per month, I suppose in Canadian dollars, to repay us for things they buy from us. And anything above those credits will be paid to Canada in gold.
The question is this, should Canadians increase their imports from Great Britain? Then that would tend to offset further purchases from us by Great Britain.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
Right. The position is
simply this, that the net deficit is financed partly out of credit and partly in cash. If the United Kingdom increases its exports of textiles, for instance, to Canada, it is just the same as United States dollars, or gold of course.
But I suggest that we do not get into a discussion of the balance of payments position on section 3 of the bill, or a discussion of any of the other thousand and one variations of this complex exchange problem, or we shall never finish. I do not know how we can handle it at all. One comes here with certain information ready to answer certain questions. I have before me some very competent officials who have figures with them, but it was not contemplated that this evening we would be discussing those subjects which have been raised. I do not think we have the necessary detailed information which could be provided to the committee. Questions as to the details in connection with permits are not properly asked now. General questions asking how permits are issued are perfectly in order, but when we get to details, it certainly does not come under this section.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: The point is well taken by the Minister of Finance. It is absolutely impossible to cover all financial ramifications on this bill. This is a bill for a definite purpose, and we are dealing with one section of it.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
The Chairman and the minister agree that this is the proper time to discuss permits; and the Minister of Trade and Commerce undertook to tell us the bases upon which he was issuing them. So far as I am concerned, the information he has given is either wrong or so confused that I, at any rate, cannot understand it. He can blame me for that, if he likes, but I will come back to have it cleared up. The minister gave us figures with regard to the automobile industry which, I think, are entirely misleading. I cannot yet believe that he has answered squarely the question I have asked him, because he got out of it by saying that exports to the United Kingdom were as good as gold, because the amount over and above our credit was paid in gold. How much is paid by our credit, and how much in gold? My understanding is that it is mainly paid by our credit. What

Foreign Exchange Conservation
is the sense of the minister saying that you apply the gold wholly to the automobile industry?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: If the British take automobiles, they will take them instead of aluminum; that is the answer to that.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: Are any credits being given to the sterling countries other than the unexpended balance of the loans today?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: None.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
As will be seen, this
section has to do with import controls. I understood-and I am speaking subject to correction-that one of the principles of import control was to provide in it the proper exceptions to enable the Minister of Trade and Commerce to assist in developing certain Canadian industries for the purpose of increasing our exports to help to overcome our balance of payments. That is the reason why I waited patiently until we reached section 3, because I thought that would be the appropriate place to discuss the positive side of the program which will be under the direction of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I still feel that it is a perfectly proper question for a member of parliament to ask, namely, that some minister of the government should indicate when we can hope to get some information about that positive side of the program.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
Section 3 has nothing to
do with the positive side of the program. The provisions with respect to capital goods in schedule 3 are there because, in the very nature of things, they do not lend themselves to quota restriction. Obviously one could not make a blanket prohibition of the importation of essential goods like machinery and structural steel. It was felt that the only practical way to deal with the importation of that class of goods as distinct from consumer goods was by the permit system. That permit system has nothing directly to do with the constructive side of the program. It might well be that one of the reasons which would govern in allowing or refusing a permit would be the fact that the project which was contemplated would contribute to our export trade, but the measure is essentially restrictive. These articles are such that they could not naturally be restricted under a quota system.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
That is a fair enough
reply, but could the minister indicate at the same time when we can discuss the positive side of the program? I am beginning to wonder if there is one.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
There is one obvious place where one could do that, and that is on the estimates of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. If there were no other place, it certainly could be done there. I think that would be an appropriate place to discuss this long-range matter. Obviously it is something that cannot be accomplished overnight, and I said that in my radio speech on November 17. I said these restrictive measures would be necessary until such time as the long-range constructive measure could be brought into effect.	The hon. member for Cape
Breton South laughs.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: You mean it is out of range.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
I think any hon. member,
on reflection, will agree that it is a pretty commonsense point of view.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
I should like to get back
to the consideration of the amendment before the committee. As I understand it, the effect of that amendment i3 to take out of the operation of this bill imports from all countries other than dollar countries. I may be wrong in my interpretation, but I understand that that is what the amendment would do if accepted.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: That is my understanding of it.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
I must say that I support wholeheartedly an amendment of that type. Frankly I do not see how many of the private members on the government side can oppose that amendment. There are three types of restrictions provided by Bill No. 3. The restrictions under schedule I are in the form of outright prohibitions which apply to all countries, dollar countries and non-dollar countries or soft money countries, as the minister calls them.
Schedule II provides for quotas. It is pertinent to note that, in setting the quota restrictions, the government has forgotten all about this non-discriminatory principle about which the minister is so boastful. Two types of country are set out, the dollar country and the non-dollar country, and each is treated in a different way. I ask the Minister of Finance to correct me if I am wrong, but my understanding is that the dollar countries are Cuba, the Dominican Republic, Guatemala, Haiti, Panama, El Salvador, Switzerland and Russia, which could hardly be described as a dollar country although she is in with the rest.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
It is not a question of being a dollar country or not. It is rather a ques-

Foreign Exchange Conservation
tion of being one of the group of countries which are technically known as countries in balance of payment difficulties.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
Then there is the United States, including Alaska, Hawaii, Guam, Puerto Rico and the Virgin Islands, and Venezuela. There is discrimination in connection with schedule II.
There is a third group which comes under the Minister of Trade and Commerce and in which goods from all countries are included. In this case a permit must be obtained for the import of capital goods from any country.
It is perfectly clear that the problem we are facing is a shortage of United States dollars. It is also perfectly clear-and no minister has contradicted this-that under the Geneva trade treaties which the minister gives as his reason for having non-discriminafcory-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: I did not give it as my reason.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: I am glad to hear that. Incidentally, I suspected that that was not the minister's reason. There is no doubt that under the Geneva treaties we have the power to adopt discriminatory policies.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: For twelve months.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: For twelve months. The minister says that this bill is temporary; he is calling it an emergency bill. The Minister of Trade and Commerce said it is to be for only a few months. Is it to be for more than twelve months, or what is it to be?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: Just keep the record straight; I never said a few months.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: I am afraid that what happens is that the Minister of Trade and Commerce gets enthusiastic and does not know what he says.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: I know what I say.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: I am afraid that statement was of that type.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: I am afraid it was not.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
It is perfectly clear that under the Geneva trade treaties Canada can discriminate to remedy an adverse exchange situation. It is perfectly clear that, by adopting this policy of total prohibition against non-dollar countries when we do not need to, we have discrimination. That is the sort of action which is breaking the terms of the agreement upon which some of the ministers place such store.
The minister said last night that this nondiscriminatory policy was of the utmost value to Canada because of our large export trade and the fact that there was this Atlantic 5849-75J
triangle of the United States, Canada and: Great Britain. I would point out that Great Britain has always been our best customer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: No.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: Practically always.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: No, not practically always.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: Ever since confederation, with the exception of a few years. So far as Great Britain is concerned, much of that trade has been built up undter the discriminatory policy. The empire preferences, which were the only things that pulled us out of the depression, were discriminatory. Under those preferences, British Columbia was able to sell her lumber, her apples and her fish. There is no British Columbia member on the Liberal side of the house who will disagree with that statement.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: Do not point at me; I voted against the trade agreements.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
You made a big mistake that time. The hon. member for New Westminster does not often make a mistake like that. The imperial preferences were discriminatory. Canada's whole tariff policy from confederation to within these last few weeks has been discriminatory. No matter what government was in power, that was the type of fiscal policy we adopted.
Now suddenly the government has turned to a non-discriminatory policy. I would point out that we do not yet know what the United States will do. Congress has not approved the Geneva treaties and we do not know yet how far they are going to go. We do not know what concessions we shall get in the United States market. For the life of me I cannot understand why Canada is in such a hurry to give everything away. The Minister of Finance said last night, at page 1088 of Hansard:
We do want to set an example.
We want to set an example to the whole world. That is why we are rushing into this non-discriminatory policy. The hon. member for Kindersley said that the government had adopted this non-discriminatory policy because of the Geneva treaties, but the Minister of Finance a moment ago denied that. He said that is not the reason at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: Not the only reason.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
The reason was given clearly by the minister himself when he said on December 9, as reported at page 95 of Hansard:
The United States in particular attaches great importance to the non-discrimination
Foreign Exchange Conservation

^principle. While it possibly could not be called -a fetish with them, it is a principle to which .great importance is attached. The success of this emergency program and the smooth functioning of our economy depend upon the wholehearted co-operation of our friends to the *south. That has been evidenced by their willingness to make us a loan of $300 million.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: And to give us oil and steel.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: Give us nothing. We are paying for it all. The minister talks about a loan of $300 million. He does not tell the house that he was turned down when he asked for $800 million.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: He did not ask for that and was not turned down. Where does my hon. friend get his information?

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: Let us get down to bedrock. The reason for this rush to adopt a nondiscriminatory policy is to please the United States, and there is no other reason. This bill has one great defect. It should have stamped on every page, in large red letters, "Made in U.S.A."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: What nonsense!

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: Then we would know exactly what sort of thing we are dealing with.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: No truck or trade with the Yankees.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: It is not a question of no truck or trade. That is just a cheap interjection.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: I am simply saying-

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: Let my hon. friend rise in his place to say it.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: I simply say that cutting off imports from the United States, a market which they have had for many years, to help us straighten out our dollar position and at the same time preserve our place in the United States market is no truck or trade with the Yankees.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
I do not know what that has to do with the matter. I do say this, Mr. Chairman: there was a situation to be met and I am sure the people of the United States understand it. They are friends of ours and they know what position we are in. They want these restrictions lifted as soon as possible, and the quickest way to remedy our trouble was to put restrictions on imports of dollar goods rather than on goods from all over the world. The United States people have always been our friends and always will be. I should like to tell the ministers this, that the people of the United States and the United States government would have far more respect for the Canadian government if

it stood on its feet and took the straightforward course. It is not the American way to want to have people grovelling before them and trying to win their favour. That is not how they do business, no more than it is our way. If we want the respect of the people of the United States, let us be open and aboveboard about this thing and not try to go around the corner. I urge the members on the government side to support this amendment and to make this bill apply only to the dollar countries. That is the reasonable provision to make at the present time. Put the bill through on that basis, and let us try to get over our difficulties as quickly as possible. But do not use this present occasion as a means of bringing in a non-discriminatory policy.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: I do not know how my hon. friend can speak with such complete assurance as to what the attitude of the United States people and government would be if we adopted the suggestion which is contained in this amendment and which my hon. friend has just advocated of a frankly out-and-out discriminatory policy against the United States.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: And all other dollar countries.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
But they do not amount to very much, I am sorry to say. It would be considered, and rightly considered, as a frankly discriminatory policy aimed at the United States. I know what I am talking about, because I have some means of knowing what the people of the United States feel about trade discrimination and I know that is how it would be considered. I hope the committee will fully realize the implications of adopting such a policy. I realize them, and I hope the committee will. The United States have been very good neighbours, and in the difficult times during the war when we were very short of essential supplies there was never any restriction placed on their exports to Canada. Export permits and export controls have never been enforced by the United States against Canada, as they have been against every other country. When hon. members stop to reflect for a moment on some of the essential raw materials we have to obtain from the United States, such as oil, steel and so on, I think they will agree it is important that the United States should continue to treat us in that wray. That is something we might well bear in mind. I have, both this afternoon and before, discussed this question of discrimination and non-discrimination, and I have said that the net effect of adhering to this desirable principle will be, not to injure or diminish our imports from soft currency areas, but to increase them.
The amendment strikes right at the fundamental principle of the bill and converts it

Foreign Exchange Conservation
from a bill which is non-discriminatory to a bill which is aimed directly at the United States. I want the members of the committee to realize fully what they are doing if they vote for this amendment. I say at once that I cannot accept it and the government cannot accept it. The amendment will be opposed.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: I should like to ask the minister a question arising out of his statement. Was the minister giving the committee an expression of his own opinion when he said that discriminatory measures against the United States would have repercussions in the way of stopping all United States exports to Canada, or has he had the assurance from United States authorities that that would be the result?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: I have had no such assurance, but I know this without any question, that such action would be deeply resented in the United States. What action they might see fit to take in consequence I do not know. They have always treated us extremely well. But to take such discriminatory action against them is something I would not do.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
I am reminded by the minister's statement of something that took place in this house in 1930 when Canada was facing an adverse trade balance with the United States, although in lesser degree than today. It is my understanding that at that time the Conservative party, then in opposition, were calling upon the government to take action to right the adverse trade balance in the then only known way by the imposition of tariffs. The government was unwilling to take this course, and the then Prime Minister who is also the present Prime Minister said: Oh, yes, we could take action like that, but in dealing with our great friends and neighbours to the south "we must keep cool heads." Somebody from the front row of the opposition benches called out that the right hon. gentleman "has his extremities mixed." I think we have the same situation here now. If the minister has not this assurance from an official source in the United States that the result of our taking direct measures to counteract what after all is shortage of United States dollars and not other currency, I think we have the same Liberal party attitude, the same pattern and no changing of its stripes after eighteen years. I feel sure that in cur present difficulties any steps that we took which were not designed against any country for the mere sake of discrimination, but were designed to protect this country from conditions to which it has come without any fault on the part of the Canadian people, would not be resented by
any right-minded people. In taking the course that he has, and in making the statements that he has made this evening, the minister is not rightly interpreting the spirit either of the United States or Canadian people.
I have been quite amazed, and I should like the minister to expand on his position in this respect. In introducing this bill, the minister gave a reason for the imposition of the special excise taxes, which may be found on page 336 of Hansard. I agree it was only one reason, but he said in part:
A second reason for these taxes was to limit so far as practicable the degree of discrimination against regular suppliers in the United States and their dealer organizations in Canada. For the time being, many of these suppliers and dealers are losing a part of their business because of the unavoidable necessity of restricting imports from the United States. Regrettable as it is, we cannot help that.
I call the attention of the committee to the next words:
But by imposing these excise taxes we are doing something to protect the legitimate long-range interests of these businesses. While the Canadian manufacturers are temporarily relieved of competition from the United States, their unexpected advantage is being at least partly offset by the effects of the special taxes.
I would have said that the Canadian manufacturers were under disadvantage now, not advantages. So much for the way the minister, in practising non-discrimination, deals with United States business which has interests in Canada. He specifically protects them. He uses the word that is so hateful to him, "protection". When he introduces this general range of legislation respecting restrictions he will protect United States business. Perhaps there is nothing wrong with that, but I would have expected that he would also take equal pains to protect Canadian businesses and the Canadian people. I would have thought he would use-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: The tax is against the Canadians also.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: I would have thought that he would use them with at least as much consideration and generosity as he used United States firms.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: He has.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
But on the other hand, I shall give the committee one example of how the minister looks at his duty toward the Canadian people. He protects the United States businessman. But when we were talking the other night about hothouse tomatoes and lettuce, the minister, in dealing with the restriction and refusing to give the Canadian people any lead as to how long the restriction
Foreign Exchange Conservation

would be in operation, said of the measure, as reported at page 1082 of Hansard of February 10:
It is put on reluctantly, and anyone who expands production in a particular field, relying on the protection which is afforded by these prohibitions, must do so at his own risk.
In other words, special measures to protect the United States business. Perhaps that is perfectly all right, but surely not all right when he accompanies them with these categorical statements that Canadians must get along at their own risk.
Then again, on page 1077 of Hansard the minister said, and he brought this point up himself in talking about representations that had been made to him:
We realize, of course, that it has a highly protective effect; and quite a number of Canadian industrialists, or at least, Canadian producers, have suggested that many United States dollars could be saved if we would add some items to the list, and thereby stimulate production in Canada. However, thus far we have not seen fit to accede to those requests.
In another part of the same evening's debate at page 1086, the minister had this to say about the suggestion from the hon. member for York West, that deflation of the dollar would still be necessary, coupled with this program. Referring to the hon. member, the minister said:
It is true that he has been an advocate of devaluation for some time, and there are a great many people in this country who would like to see the devaluation of the dollar. They would benefit by it.
Some hon. members interjected, suggesting that that was an unworthy statement for the minister to make, and he went on and said:
Yes, they would; I know they would; make no mistake about that. There are advocates of devaluation because, among other things, it would benefit some lines of endeavour that they would be in.
His attitude throughout seems to have been one of being willing to get away from the Liberal party's doctrinaire free trade, and even lo use the horrible word "protection" in respect of the United States manufacturer; but when it comes down to helping Canadian producers, in our present difficult situation to expand the production of goods in this country, to get some advantage of what otherwise must be disadvantages to all of us in Canada he says, No; it is at their own risk. They have private reasons of their own benefit for making these requests. Altogether, Mr. Chairman, not only on the ground of this question of discrimination, of stopping imports from non-dollar countries, but also on the ground of what right the minister has to ignore the interests of Canadian producers

when he carefully protects the interests of United States producers, I think we should hear more from him.
The hon. member for Vancouver South has quoted the passage where the minister said that in this measure we want to set an example to the world. I want to suggest to the minister that his first duty is to the Canadian people and to Canadian business. We are in difficulties which are not of our own creation. We have no duty to set examples which will react against our own people. I want to suggest to him that he is still Minister of Finance in a Canadian government, and that we have not yet the wider form of North American government or world government which he seems to envisage by his statements to the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: I will just answer that, if I may. We are still on this protection business. I have dealt with this time and time again. The effect of imposing these prohibitions is about the highest form of protection that could be imposed. It protects the domestic producers who are behind the embargo, including the raising of vegetables or anything else. The statement that I made about these taxes and preserving to the legitimate United States exporter the market which he has had in Canada was this. It would offset to some extent the terrifically grave disadvantage under which he was placed in this market by the high protection we were giving to the Canadian domestic producer. Such offsetting protection, if one may call it that, of the United States exporter to Canada, is more than outweighed by the highly protective advantage given to the domestic producer. To say that you are protecting the United States exporter by cutting him down on a quota basis to a fraction of what he had previously and giving the Canadian producer a free and unrestricted market is a distortion of the real truth. There is no question as to the excise tax conferring protection on the United States exporter.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: You yourself used the word.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
How does a country prosper unless it has export and import trade? If anyone in this house will suggest that we should do anything which would unnecessarily injure the normal flow of trade between our two countries, he has a political philosophy which is completely different from my own. This afternoon a number of hon. members were urging the view that we were foolish in cutting off imports. The hon. member for Swift Current was urging that we should remove some of these prohibitions and should

Foreign Exchange Conservation
let in some of these refrigerators. You cannot have it both ways in these things. To suggest that this policy is one which shows I have just forgotten the exact language my hon. friend used-that I am thinking of world government, international government-[DOT]

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: North American.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

What country in the world has a bigger stake in the rebuilding of the export trade of Great Britain, France, the Scandinavian countries and other countries in the soft currency area than has Canada? What country has a greater stake? None. It means a great deal to Canada right now to help those countries in every way possible to increase their export trade. That is the only way, under present conditions, that we are going to help to get ourselves paid.
The kind of treatment the minister is proposing does not simply harm the United States and harm these other countries. It is harming a great many Canadians right here at home. Let me give one or two examples. I am thinking of two young returned soldiers in Toronto who took everything they had in the world, including their re-establishment grants, to establish here an agency for the importation of a certain line of French goods, based upon contacts that those veterans had made when they were fighting in France. What happened? What will happen now? This bill, simply because the Minister of Finance blindly follows the fetish of non-discrimination, will completely ruin the business of those two young veterans. Will any man in his

right senses stand in this House of Commons and1 say that will help the United States?
Mr. Chairman, I could give you dozens of examples of other veterans and other Canadians who have established import businesses in Canada for the purpose of importing goods from Great Britain, from the commonwealth countries and from other countries in Europe- soft currency countries. What is happening to them? They are being ruined. Their businesses are being completely mined by this measure. Why? Will that bring help to the United States? Of course it will not. Will that appease sentiment in the United States? -to ruin the businesses of these Canadian importers, and to reduce imports from these soft currency countries which so badly need to export today?
Well, if that is the kind of sentiment the Minister of Finance imputes to our cousins over the border, then I say to him and to the committee that he insults the intelligence of the people of the United States.
This situation with which we are confronted, which is embodied in the arbitrary and dictatorial measures in this bill, is a situation brought upon this country by a government that was blind and impotent. What they are doing today, now, is not simply to encompass further ruin of the Canadian -people; rather, by making such a stupid fetish of this talk of non-discrimination, they are doing untold damage to our relations with trading nations elsewhere in the world, with which in the future we are bound intimately to be connected, if there is to be any hope of economic revival in the world.
Two wrongs do make a right; and the Minister of Finance does not make this bill one whit more acceptable to the house or to the Canadian people by extending the harm that it does to the soft currency areas, as he is doing to the hard currency areas. The more one hears the government trying to support this measure, the more one is convinced that the whole thing is a priceless example of economic lunacy.

We have export controls on feed grain which we are enforcing against the United States. For certain reasons the United States is not enforcing her export controls against Canada with respect to steel and oil. She is entitled to exercise those controls under the Geneva and other agreements.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: Would you say that is discriminatory?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
It all depends upon how one defines "discriminatory". Under the Geneva agreements, one is not permitted to pay export subsidies, and the United States are not paying export subsidies. However,

one is permitted to exercise export control over commodities in short supply in the country of origin, and that is what the United States are doing today. However, they are not exercising those export controls against this country and never have done so.
There is one other feature I did not touch on in discussing this matter. This is only my personal opinion which may or may not be shared by others, but I feel that, while the European recovery plan is under discussion in congress, which is a far-reaching and generous plan on the part of the United States and which we understand contemplates the use of the United States taxpayers' money to purchase supplies in other countries, it would be most unfortunate if her next door neighbour were to adopt a discriminatory policy against her.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
It is warmer in the chamber this evening than it was yesterday afternoon, and there is a little more humour. Both of these conditions appear to be welcomed on all sides because they help to break the monotony. I am glad to feel so much heat and see so much interest and hear so much humour. During the debate tonight on the amendment, I think some of those who have defended the amendment and some who have opposed it have gone farther than the case warrants.
I wish to say a word in favour of the amendment, but I want to say also that I am not a preferentialist. I think there are some good principles embodied in the Geneva treaties which were signed by twenty-one nations. There are in those treaties certain general principles with which I think this committee agrees. We believe in multilateral agreements. The more multilateral they can be, the better. But there are realistic positions that have to be taken into consideration. The agreement itself and those who drafted the agreement recognize that a country like Canada might find itself in a position where it had to protect its currency, and so provision was made for that very purpose so that until a certain date in 1949 we could take advantage of the discriminatory clause.
All that we are saying in this amendment is that we want to take advantage of that discriminatory clause which was put into the Geneva agreement, and thus we are not violating its principle. We are simply taking care of our own people and protecting our own interests in the best way we possibly can.
As has been pointed out, I think very ably by the hon. member for Eglinton, such a policy need not and, I believe, would not

affect our relationship with the United States one little bit. If it did, it would not be to the credit of the United States. Most decidedly if their dollar was in jeopardy or their exchange was in the position of ours they would not hesitate for one moment-and I do not blame them-to take advantage of the discriminatory clause. We are merely asking that, because we are banning certain goods from the United States under certain conditions, we shall not ban those goods from Britain or from the dominions or from any other country that might want to supply us with them. By so doing, we would make it possible for the people of Canada to secure from Britain and the dominions the goods we have found it necessary to ban from the United States. In the second place, we would improve our exchange position with the United States, and ultimately perhaps would have more to expend in the United States and might shorten the period for which this legislation is necessary, assuming that the government's predictions are correct that it will be only a temporary measure. But may I say that I doubt its temporary character.
I am one of those who believe that, whether we iike it or not-and we are not blaming the government for this-the world situation is such that there may be a reorientation of the whole business of international relationships and international trade, and what we think today may be only for a brief duration of a month or two may be merely the beginning of a long period of very much different relationships among the nations of the world in matters of trade.
And so, having in view, in the first place, the needs of our own people in respect of goods, and having regard, in the second place, to the actual financial problem with which this nation is confronted, I and those on this side who support the amendment cannot see what harm could come to our relationship with the United States by adopting the amendment. But we can see that great good can come to this country and to other countries in Europe which might be glad to make exchanges with us. So I urge the government to accept the amendment, and if they will not accept it I hope we shall be able to carry it anyway, and thus materially improve the legislation which the government is proposing.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, dealing with the amendment on its merits, I should like to reply to the arguments advanced against it by the Minister of Finance and the hon. member for New Westminster.
In opposing the amendment, the Minister of Finance based his argument almost
entirely on the premise that to adopt it could be interpreted only as being directly discriminatory against the United States. That, to my mind, is losing sight of the main purpose of this legislation, which is that Canada is suffering from a shortage of United States dollars-that is not our fault-and in taking steps to relieve that shortage is not discriminating against the United States, but in essence is trying to protect our own position.
But what it seems to me is discriminatory and directly discriminatory, is to go on from there and say that, because we have to take measures to restrict our imports from the United States, we shall also apply those measures to the other countries of the world. That is discrimination against the other countries of the world, whereas the original measure, which apparently was acceptable to the United States, is not discriminating against them, because in essence it is something that was simply forced upon us to protect our own position. If, then, the United States are willing to accept the fact that we have to impose an embargo on trade with them it seems to me that they will not ask that we do the same thing which would hurt our trade with the rest of the world in the same way that we hurt our trade with them. If, as the minister says, they are good neighbours and realize our difficulties and have accepted the fact that we are reluctantly compelled to do this, they would not say: Then you must do the same thing to the rest of the world that you are doing to us. That, I am certain, is not the position which the United States would take, as the minister suggested to justify the stand which the government has adopted as a result of its doctrinaire belief in the policy of non-discrimination. It cannot be interpreted in any other way.
The hon. member for New Westminster advanced, I think, a more cogent reason against accepting the amendment if his argument had been correct, but it was not correct. He dealt with the suggestion of the hon. member for Vancouver South that the embargoes contained in the bill are damaging to our trade with the United Kingdom. The hon. member for New Westminster said: Let us look at schedule I; and the hon. member for Fraser Valley did the same thing. They picked out a few items such as turtles and nuts in the shell and out of the shell, and so on. Of course it is a very easy thing to pick out three or four items from a schedule of eight pages and say: These articles do not come in here from the United Kingdom and therefore this bill will not hurt our trade with
