the United Kingdom. But if you will look at schedule I a little more carefully and com-ipare its items with the goods which the United Kingdom is prepared to supply, it is .obvious that this bill would damage our trade with the United Kingdom and the British commonwealth extensively. I should like to name just a few articles.
On December 11 the British government published a list of articles which it was prepared. to supply in quantity to Canada in 1948. They include lighting fixtures, office furniture, domestic laundry machines, refrigerators, movie projectors, electric clocks, camera and photographic accessories, domestic electric appliances-all substantial articles covering a wide variety of trade. These are the articles which the United Kingdom is prepared to supply to Canada in quantity in 1948.
Schedule I contains a list of goods the importation of which is prohibited, and at the bottom of page 9 you will find this item: kitchen or household hollow-ware. There is a category of kitchen articles. On page 10 of the bill appears "refrigerators, domestic or store, completely equipped or not; motion picture projectors for use with films; lamp shades and shade holders; electric light fixtures or parts." Then two-thirds down the page a whole category of electric appliances, domestic electric appliances such as are covered1 in the list that the United. Kingdom is prepared to supply. On page 11 of the bill, still in schedule I, item 519 is as follows, "house, office, cabinet or store furniture of wood, iron or other material", and so on. These are not items of trade lightly to be dismissed as the hon. member for New Westminster and the hon. member for Eraser Valley tried to dismiss them. They are substantial items of trade. They are not like nuts or turtles or anything else one wishes to name. They are items of importance to the United Kingdom, which is striving so earnestly to increase her exports to us, and which we should be encouraging to increase its exports so that we might enable it to pay us in dollars for what we must sell to it.
This situation is one which has been forced on us by circumstances; and if, as the minister says, the United States is willing to recognize our position, and not to hold it against us then-and I repeat the argument put forward by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard- the minister's first duty is to the people of Canada. His first duty is to minimize-

speechtext: That is what I am trying to do in proposing a non-diseriminatory bill.

That is exactly what the minister is not doing in proposing a non-

discriminatory bill. He calls it a nondiscriminatory bill, but that does not make it so. Actually it is a discriminatory bill, unnecessarily discriminating against the commonwealth countries, France, Belgium, The Netherlands, Luxembourg, the Scandinavian countries, and all the other countries in the soft currency areas which need not be included in this bill. It is discriminatory against them, and to that extent it is unnecessarily injurious to the Canadian people and the Canadian economy. If the minister and hon. members opposite would see the matter in that light, which is a logical approach to the question, and if, as he says, and as we believe, the United States is realistic about the matter, then it could easily be seen that the amendment .proposed by the hon. member for Kindersley is acceptable. It is simply making what is otherwise an unnecessarily cumbersome and harsh piece of legislation into a good, workable and realistic piece of legislation.

Sitting on this side of the house, I cannot speak for the policy of my party. I can follow the policy of the party when we come to one. So far as I know, the policy of this party has never been to uphold this amendment. I believe it would be a mistake if this amendment were to carry. It seems to me that there is no particular reason why it should carry. This is a bad bill. I spoke about it when it was up for second reading, and this amendment will not make a bad bill any better; I think it will make it far worse. The effect of this amendment will be to do something that will be injurious to us as a country. I can only wish that the debate which has taken place in the last two hours had not taken place at all.
Somebody spoke about what happened in 1930. The year 1930 is not a long time ago so far as I am concerned; it is comparatively recent history, but a great many things have happened during that time. So far as I am concerned, I will oppose the amendment.

If a flag is thf symbol of nationhood, and if we have any pride in our nation, is it not better to stand on our feet than to go down on our knees to somebody?
I 'do not know whether the United States want this or not, since some people say they do not and others say they do. But from appearances, this is influenced by the United States. I think the minister is heavily influenced by them in this matter, and to me it can be reduced just as simply as this. An individual owes money to his storekeeper. He has not been able to pay his bill because of some circumstances in his business that cut down his earning power. He goes to the storekeeper and says, "I owe you more money than I can pay for some time; therefore I will have to cut down on my purchases from you." The storekeeper would simply say, "Certainly you will have to do that", and it would be an amicable agreement. But if the individual who owed the storekeeper money was associated with some other person who owed him money and had some goods that the debtor of the other storekeeper could use, and the merchant to whom the individual owed money were to say, "If you do not buy from me you cannot take anything in payment from another person," I would say that that would be an unfriendly act on the part of the merchant who was the creditor of the original person of whom I spoke.
